title: Indian Couple in Canada Earns Over Rs 1 Lakh Delivering Food for Seven Days
excerpt: Ruman and Tarun grossed CAD 1,447 on Uber Eats in a week-long challenge, spending about CAD 35 a day on fuel and stressing it was an experiment, not their regular job.
body:
• Indian couple Ruman and Tarun delivered food on Uber Eats in Canada for seven days as an experiment and earned CAD 1,447, about Rs 1,02,013, according to coverage of their video.
  • The headline figure is gross: they spent about CAD 35 a day on fuel, roughly CAD 245 across the week, and carried meals from home to keep food costs down.
  • The couple stressed this was a fun experiment, not their regular job, and said being selective about which orders to accept, weighing distance against pay, was central to hitting the total.
  • For readers weighing gig delivery: at CAD 35 a day in fuel alone, the week's fuel bill consumed about 17 per cent of gross earnings before any other vehicle or tax costs.

An Indian couple living in Canada set themselves a simple question: could two people earn Rs 1 lakh in a single week by delivering food? Ruman and Tarun took on the challenge on Uber Eats for seven days and documented it on video, a story first reported by NDTV Food and covered by News18 and Moneycontrol.

They cleared the target. Over the seven days the couple earned CAD 1,447, about Rs 1,02,013, according to a synthesis of the News18 and Moneycontrol coverage. It is a striking headline number for a week's gig work, and it is also a gross figure, which is where the details they shared matter more than the total.

What the week actually cost

The couple said they spent around CAD 35 a day on fuel while completing deliveries. Across seven days that is about CAD 245 in fuel alone, roughly 17 per cent of the CAD 1,447 they grossed, before vehicle wear, insurance or taxes enter the calculation. They also brought meals from home while they were out delivering, a small decision that kept a daily food spend from eating into the experiment's earnings.

Their other lesson was about selectivity. Rather than accepting every order the app offered, they advised choosing orders deliberately, weighing the pay against the distance involved. In app-based delivery, a low-paying order that takes a driver far from busy restaurant clusters costs twice: once in fuel and time on that trip, and again in the better-paying orders missed while returning.

"An Indian couple living in Canada set themselves a simple question: could two people earn Rs 1 lakh in a single week by delivering food?"

An experiment, not a payslip

The couple were clear about what the week was and was not. They described it as a fun experiment, not their regular job, and the format itself shapes the result: a challenge video compresses a best-effort week, worked deliberately and tracked carefully, into a single number. It does not show a slow week, a week with a vehicle repair, or what the same hours pay across a month.

That distinction is the useful part for diaspora readers in Canada weighing delivery work as a side income. The experiment shows the ceiling a focused week can reach on a major platform, and it shows the arithmetic underneath it: fuel at CAD 35 a day, home-packed meals instead of bought ones, and disciplined order selection. Anyone running the same test for real should run those same numbers on their own city, car and schedule before treating a viral total as an expectation.

The video has drawn attention precisely because it makes gig earnings concrete. Most delivery income claims online are either app marketing or complaints. A couple publishing their gross, their fuel cost and their method, and labelling the whole thing an experiment, gives viewers something rarer: a number they can actually interrogate.
